chapter: Measuring Space: Perimeter and Area (Class 9 Maths)
note: 50 mixed-form items across the chapter's concepts. Difficulty 17 Easy / 17 Medium / 16 Hard.

items.stem: The perimeter of a closed figure is the total length of
items.explanation: Perimeter is the distance all the way round the boundary of the figure.

options.why: A diagonal crosses the interior and is not part of the boundary.
Height is a single measurement, not the distance round.
Area measures the surface enclosed, not the distance round it.

items.stem: The circumference of a circle of radius r is
items.explanation: The circumference is 2 times pi times the radius.

options.why: That is the formula for the area, not the circumference.
This is half the circumference, the length of a semicircular arc.
This doubles the correct circumference.

items.stem: The area of a circle of radius r is
items.explanation: The area is pi times the square of the radius.

options.why: That is the circumference, a length rather than an area.
Using the diameter without dividing by four gives four times too much.
This doubles the correct area.

items.stem: A triangle has base 10 cm and height 6 cm. Its area is
items.explanation: The area is half the base times the height, that is half of 60.

options.why: This omits the factor of one half.
This adds the base and height instead of multiplying.
This halves the answer once too often.

items.stem: The number pi is defined as the ratio of a circle's
items.explanation: Pi is the circumference divided by the diameter, and the ratio is the same for every circle.

options.why: That ratio is pi times the radius, so it varies with the circle.
That ratio is always exactly 2.
That ratio is one divided by 2 pi, not pi.

items.stem: Heron's formula is most useful when a triangle is given by
items.explanation: It computes area from the three side lengths alone, without needing any height.

options.why: With base and height the simpler half base times height formula applies.
That case is handled by trigonometry rather than Heron's formula.
The perimeter alone does not determine the area of a triangle.

items.stem: A sector of angle 90 degrees is cut from a circle. Its area is what fraction of the circle?
items.explanation: 90 degrees is a quarter of 360 degrees, so the sector is a quarter of the circle.

options.why: A half would need a sector angle of 180 degrees.
A third would need a sector angle of 120 degrees.
An eighth would need a sector angle of 45 degrees.

items.concept: Median of a Triangle Divides Area
items.stem: A median of a triangle divides it into two triangles of
items.explanation: The two triangles have equal bases, since the median bisects a side, and share the same height, so their areas are equal.

options.why: That ratio applies to the two parts of a median cut by the centroid, not to the areas.
The two triangles generally have different perimeters.
Equal bases and a common height force the areas to be equal.

items.stem: The value 22 divided by 7 is used for pi because it is
items.explanation: It is a convenient rational approximation; pi itself is irrational and cannot equal any fraction.

options.why: Pi is irrational, so no fraction can equal it exactly.
22 by 7 is 3.142857..., which is slightly larger than pi.
3.14 and 355 by 113 are also used, the latter far more accurately.

items.stem: Brahmagupta's formula gives the area of a quadrilateral that is
items.explanation: It applies to a cyclic quadrilateral, one whose four vertices lie on a circle.

options.why: Four side lengths alone do not fix the area unless the shape is cyclic.
The formula is far more general than that.
The formula does not require a pair of parallel sides.

items.stem: Why are perimeter and area measured in different kinds of unit?
items.answer: Perimeter is a length, so it is measured in units such as centimetres. Area measures a surface, which needs two dimensions, so it is measured in square units such as square centimetres.

items.stem: Find the circumference of a circle of radius 7 cm, taking pi as 22 by 7.
items.answer: Circumference is 2 pi r, which is 2 times 22 by 7 times 7, and the sevens cancel to give 44 cm.

items.stem: Find the area of a circle of radius 7 cm, taking pi as 22 by 7.
items.answer: Area is pi r squared, which is 22 by 7 times 49. One seven cancels, leaving 22 times 7, which is 154 square cm.

items.stem: What fraction of the circumference is an arc of 60 degrees?
items.answer: One sixth, because 60 degrees is 60 out of 360 degrees, and that fraction simplifies to one sixth.

items.stem: State Heron's formula, defining every symbol.
items.answer: The area equals the square root of s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c), where a, b and c are the three side lengths and s is the semi-perimeter, that is half of a plus b plus c.

items.stem: What does it mean to square a rectangle?
items.answer: It means constructing a square whose area is exactly equal to that of the given rectangle. For a rectangle of sides a and b, the square must have side equal to the square root of ab, the geometric mean of the two sides.

items.stem: Why can the circumference of a circle with a whole-number diameter never be a whole number?
items.answer: The circumference is pi times the diameter. Since pi is irrational, multiplying it by any non-zero whole number gives an irrational result, and an irrational number is never a whole number.

items.stem: Two sectors have the same angle but different radii. How do their areas compare?
items.answer: The areas are in the ratio of the squares of the radii, not of the radii themselves, because sector area is a fixed fraction of pi r squared. Doubling the radius therefore quadruples the area.

items.stem: Explain the difference between perimeter and area, with an example showing that one can change while the other stays the same.
items.answer: Perimeter is the total length of the boundary of a figure and is measured in units of length. Area is the amount of surface enclosed and is measured in square units. They are independent enough that one can change while the other does not. Consider rectangles of perimeter 20 cm. A rectangle of 6 cm by 4 cm has area 24 square cm, while one of 9 cm by 1 cm has area 9 square cm, and one of 5 cm by 5 cm has area 25 square cm. All three have the same perimeter but very different areas, and the square gives the largest area. The general lesson is that knowing the perimeter does not determine the area.

items.stem: Explain why the area of a triangle is half the base times the height.
items.answer: Take any triangle and make an identical copy of it. Rotate the copy by half a turn and join it to the original along one side. The two together form a parallelogram whose base is the base of the triangle and whose height is the height of the triangle. The area of a parallelogram is base times height, and the parallelogram is made of exactly two congruent triangles, so each triangle has half that area. Hence the area of a triangle is half the base times the height. The height must be the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite vertex, not the length of a slanted side, because that is the height of the parallelogram.

items.stem: Find the area of a triangle whose sides are 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm.
items.answer: The semi-perimeter s is half of 13 plus 14 plus 15, that is half of 42, which is 21 cm. Then s minus a is 21 minus 13, which is 8; s minus b is 21 minus 14, which is 7; and s minus c is 21 minus 15, which is 6. Heron's formula gives the area as the square root of 21 times 8 times 7 times 6. The product is 21 times 8 = 168, times 7 = 1176, times 6 = 7056. The square root of 7056 is 84. The area is therefore 84 square cm.

items.stem: A sector of a circle of radius 14 cm has an angle of 90 degrees. Find its area and arc length, taking pi as 22 by 7.
items.answer: The sector is 90 out of 360 degrees, which is one quarter of the circle. The full area is pi r squared, that is 22 by 7 times 196, which is 616 square cm. A quarter of this is 154 square cm. The full circumference is 2 pi r, that is 2 times 22 by 7 times 14, which is 88 cm. A quarter of this is 22 cm. So the sector has area 154 square cm and arc length 22 cm. Note that the perimeter of the sector would also include the two radii, giving 22 plus 14 plus 14, that is 50 cm.

items.stem: Derive a formula for the length of an arc subtending an angle of theta degrees in a circle of radius r.
items.answer: The whole circle corresponds to 360 degrees and has circumference 2 pi r. An arc of theta degrees is the fraction theta divided by 360 of the whole circle, and arc length is proportional to the angle at the centre. So the arc length is theta divided by 360, times 2 pi r. As a check, putting theta equal to 360 gives the full circumference 2 pi r, and putting theta equal to 180 gives pi r, the length of a semicircular arc, both of which are correct. The same reasoning with area in place of circumference gives the sector area as theta divided by 360, times pi r squared.

items.concept: Median of a Triangle Divides Area
items.stem: Prove that a median of a triangle divides it into two triangles of equal area.
items.answer: Let ABC be a triangle and let AD be the median from A, so that D is the midpoint of BC. Consider the two triangles ABD and ACD. Take BD and DC as their bases. These are equal, because D is the midpoint of BC. Now drop the perpendicular from A to the line BC, meeting it at H. The same segment AH is the height of both triangles ABD and ACD, because both have their bases along the same line BC and share the vertex A. Since the area of a triangle is half the base times the height, and the two triangles have equal bases and the same height, their areas are equal. Hence the median AD divides triangle ABC into two triangles of equal area. Note that this does not depend on the triangle being isosceles, and the two halves generally have different shapes and perimeters.

items.stem: Explain why the side of a square equal in area to a rectangle of sides a and b is the square root of ab, and why this length can always be constructed.
items.answer: If the square has side x then its area is x squared, and for the areas to be equal we need x squared equal to ab, so x is the square root of ab. This is the geometric mean of a and b. It can always be constructed with straight edge and compass. Draw a straight line and mark on it consecutive segments of lengths a and b, so the total length is a plus b. Draw a semicircle on that whole segment as diameter. At the point where a meets b, erect a perpendicular to meet the semicircle at P. The length of that perpendicular is exactly the square root of ab. The reason is the angle in a semicircle: the triangle formed with the diameter is right-angled at P, and in a right-angled triangle the altitude to the hypotenuse is the geometric mean of the two parts into which it divides the hypotenuse. So the construction turns an area problem into the circle theorem, and shows that a square can always be made equal in area to any given rectangle.

items.stem: Discuss what it means in practice that pi is irrational.
items.answer: It means pi cannot be written as a ratio of two whole numbers, so its decimal expansion never ends and never falls into a repeating pattern. In practice this has three consequences. First, every numerical value used for pi is an approximation: 22 by 7 is correct to two decimal places, 3.14159 to five, and 355 by 113 to six, but none is exact. Second, any calculation involving pi carries a rounding error that must be judged against the accuracy required, which is why an answer should be left in terms of pi when exactness matters. Third, certain classical problems become impossible: squaring the circle with straight edge and compass cannot be done, because it would require constructing a length involving pi, and no such construction exists. What irrationality does not mean is that pi is uncertain or approximate in itself. It is a perfectly definite number, exactly the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter; the limitation is in writing it as a decimal, not in knowing it.

items.stem: Assertion (A): The circumference of a circle is proportional to its radius. Reason (R): Circumference equals 2 pi r, and 2 pi is a constant. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and a constant multiplier is exactly what proportionality means.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: A constant multiplier is precisely the definition of proportional.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: The formula and the constancy of 2 pi are both correct.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Doubling the radius doubles the circumference exactly.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Doubling the radius doubles the area of a circle. Reason (R): Area equals pi r squared. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true but the assertion is false: since the radius is squared, doubling it multiplies the area by four.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: The squared radius means the factor is four, not two.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: The area formula pi r squared is correct.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Doubling r gives pi times 4 r squared, four times the area.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Heron's formula can find the area of any triangle. Reason (R): Three side lengths determine a triangle uniquely. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and the uniqueness of a triangle from its three sides is exactly why its area is determined by them.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: Uniqueness from three sides is precisely what makes the area computable.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Side-side-side congruence establishes that three sides fix a triangle.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Heron's formula needs only the three sides, which any triangle has.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Two shapes with equal perimeter have equal area. Reason (R): Perimeter and area both measure size. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both statements fail: perimeter does not determine area, and the two measure different things, one a length and one a surface.

options.text: Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: A 9 by 1 rectangle and a 5 by 5 square share a perimeter of 20 with areas 9 and 25.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: The counter-example above defeats the assertion as well.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Length and surface are different quantities, so the reason fails too.

items.stem: State whether true or false: the circumference of a circle is 2 pi r.
items.explanation: This is the standard formula for the distance round a circle.

options.why: 2 pi r is the circumference; pi r squared is the area.

items.stem: State whether true or false: the value of pi depends on the size of the circle.
items.explanation: Pi is the same ratio for every circle, however large or small.

options.why: The circumference-to-diameter ratio is identical for all circles.

items.stem: State whether true or false: two triangles on the same base and between the same parallels have equal area.
items.explanation: Equal bases and the same perpendicular height force the areas to be equal, whatever the shapes.

options.why: Between the same parallels the height is the same, and the base is shared, so the areas match.

items.stem: State whether true or false: trebling the radius of a circle trebles its area.
items.explanation: Since the radius is squared, trebling it multiplies the area by nine.

options.why: Area is pi r squared, so a factor of 3 on r gives a factor of 9 on the area.

items.stem: The ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter is denoted by ___________.
items.answer: pi

items.stem: The area of a circle of radius r is ___________.
items.answer: pi r squared

items.stem: In Heron's formula, s stands for the ___________ of the triangle.
items.answer: semi-perimeter, that is half the sum of the three sides

items.stem: A sector of angle 120 degrees is one ___________ of the whole circle.
items.answer: third

items.stem: Collect the formulae for perimeter and area of the main plane figures you have studied, and state the units of each.
items.answer: For a rectangle of length l and breadth b, the perimeter is 2 times (l plus b) and the area is l times b. For a square of side a, the perimeter is 4a and the area is a squared. For a triangle, the perimeter is the sum of the three sides, and the area is half the base times the perpendicular height, or by Heron's formula the square root of s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c) where s is the semi-perimeter. For a circle of radius r, the perimeter, called the circumference, is 2 pi r and the area is pi r squared. For a sector of angle theta degrees in a circle of radius r, the arc length is theta over 360 times 2 pi r and the area is theta over 360 times pi r squared. For a cyclic quadrilateral with sides a, b, c and d, Brahmagupta's formula gives the area as the square root of (s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d). In every case the perimeter or arc length is a length and is measured in units such as cm or m, while every area is measured in square units such as square cm or square m.

items.stem: A triangular field has sides 40 m, 24 m and 32 m. Find its area two different ways and comment.
items.answer: First by Heron's formula. The semi-perimeter s is half of 40 plus 24 plus 32, that is half of 96, which is 48 m. Then s minus the sides are 8, 24 and 16. The area is the square root of 48 times 8 times 24 times 16. Grouping, 48 times 8 is 384 and 24 times 16 is 384, so the product is 384 squared and the square root is exactly 384 square m. Second by the base and height formula. Notice that 24 squared plus 32 squared equals 576 plus 1024, which is 1600, and that is 40 squared. By the converse of the Pythagoras theorem the triangle is right-angled, with the two shorter sides perpendicular to each other. Taking 32 m as the base and 24 m as the height, the area is half of 32 times 24, which is half of 768, that is 384 square m. The two methods agree, which is a good check. The comment worth making is that Heron's formula always works from the sides alone, while the simpler formula became available only because the triangle turned out to be right-angled, which the side lengths revealed.

items.stem: Compare Heron's formula and Brahmagupta's formula, explaining what each needs and why the quadrilateral case requires an extra condition.
items.answer: Heron's formula gives the area of a triangle as the square root of s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c), where s is the semi-perimeter. It needs only the three side lengths, and that is sufficient because three side lengths determine a triangle completely: by the side-side-side congruence criterion, any two triangles with the same three sides are congruent and so have the same area. Brahmagupta's formula gives the area of a quadrilateral as the square root of (s - a)(s - b)(s - c)(s - d), with s again the semi-perimeter, and the resemblance to Heron's formula is striking. But it requires the quadrilateral to be cyclic, that is to have all four vertices on a circle. The extra condition is needed because four side lengths do not determine a quadrilateral. A four-bar linkage with fixed side lengths can be flexed through many shapes, all with the same perimeter but different areas, so no formula in the sides alone could give the area of an arbitrary quadrilateral. Requiring the quadrilateral to be cyclic pins down the shape, and in fact the cyclic arrangement is the one with the greatest area for those four sides. Setting d equal to zero in Brahmagupta's formula recovers Heron's formula exactly, which shows the triangle as the degenerate case of a cyclic quadrilateral with one side shrunk away.

items.stem: Among all rectangles of a fixed perimeter, which has the greatest area? Investigate and justify your conclusion.
items.answer: Take a fixed perimeter of 20 cm, so that the length and breadth add to 10 cm. Tabulating, 1 by 9 gives area 9, 2 by 8 gives 16, 3 by 7 gives 21, 4 by 6 gives 24, and 5 by 5 gives 25 square cm. The area rises to a maximum when the two sides are equal and falls away symmetrically on either side, so the square gives the greatest area. To justify it generally, let the sides be x and (10 minus x), so the area is A = x(10 minus x) = 10x minus x squared. Completing the square gives A = 25 minus (x minus 5) squared. Since a square is never negative, the largest possible value of A is 25, achieved exactly when x equals 5, that is when the rectangle is a square. The same argument with perimeter 2p shows the maximum area is p squared over 4 at the square. It is worth noting the wider pattern: among all plane figures of a given perimeter, the circle encloses the greatest area, and the square is merely the best that can be done when the shape is restricted to rectangles. This is why a fixed length of fencing encloses most ground when laid out as a circle, and why the practical answer depends on what shapes are allowed.

items.stem: Find the area of a triangle with base 18 cm and height 9 cm.
items.answer: Area is half the base times the height, that is half of 18 times 9. This gives half of 162, which is 81 square cm.

items.stem: A circular track has circumference 176 m. Find its radius, taking pi as 22 by 7.
items.answer: Circumference is 2 pi r, so 176 = 2 times 22 by 7 times r, that is 176 = 44r by 7. Multiplying both sides by 7 gives 1232 = 44r, so r = 1232 divided by 44, which is 28 m. The radius of the track is 28 m.

items.stem: A sector of a circle of radius 21 cm has an arc length of 22 cm. Find its angle and area, taking pi as 22 by 7.
items.answer: The full circumference is 2 pi r, that is 2 times 22 by 7 times 21, which is 132 cm. The arc is 22 cm, so the sector is 22 divided by 132 of the circle, which simplifies to one sixth. An angle of one sixth of 360 degrees is 60 degrees. For the area, the full circle is pi r squared, that is 22 by 7 times 441, which is 1386 square cm. One sixth of this is 231 square cm. As a check, the sector area also equals half the arc length times the radius, that is half of 22 times 21, which is 231 square cm, confirming the answer by an independent route.

items.stem: Match each figure in Column I with its area formula in Column II. Column I: (a) circle of radius r, (b) square of side a, (c) triangle of base b and height h, (d) rectangle of sides l and w. Column II: (i) half b h, (ii) l w, (iii) pi r squared, (iv) a squared.
items.answer: (a) circle - (iii) pi r squared. (b) square - (iv) a squared. (c) triangle - (i) half b h. (d) rectangle - (ii) l w.

items.stem: Match each sector angle in Column I with the fraction of the circle in Column II. Column I: (a) 45 degrees, (b) 90 degrees, (c) 120 degrees, (d) 180 degrees. Column II: (i) one third, (ii) one half, (iii) one eighth, (iv) one quarter.
items.answer: (a) 45 degrees - (iii) one eighth. (b) 90 degrees - (iv) one quarter. (c) 120 degrees - (i) one third. (d) 180 degrees - (ii) one half.

items.stem: Describe and draw the construction of a square equal in area to a given rectangle of sides a and b.
items.answer: Draw a straight line and mark on it a segment AB of length a, then immediately beyond it a segment BC of length b, so that AC has length a plus b. Find the midpoint O of AC by constructing the perpendicular bisector of AC. With centre O and radius OA, draw a semicircle on AC as diameter, on one side of the line. At the point B, erect a perpendicular to AC, and let it meet the semicircle at P. Label the length BP as x. Then the required square has side BP. To finish, construct a square on BP using perpendiculars at each end. Annotate the diagram with the reason: the angle APC stands in a semicircle and so is a right angle, and in a right-angled triangle the altitude from the right angle to the hypotenuse is the geometric mean of the two parts of the hypotenuse, so BP squared equals AB times BC, that is x squared equals ab. Since the square has area x squared and the rectangle has area ab, the two areas are equal.

items.concept: Median of a Triangle Divides Area
items.stem: Draw a triangle with all three medians and annotate the diagram to show how the six small triangles compare in area.
items.answer: Draw a scalene triangle ABC so the result is not disguised by symmetry. Find the midpoints of the three sides by constructing perpendicular bisectors, and label them D on BC, E on CA and F on AB. Draw the three medians AD, BE and CF, and label their common point G, the centroid. The medians cut the triangle into six small triangles; label them all. Annotate the diagram in stages. First, median AD divides ABC into two triangles ABD and ACD of equal area, since BD equals DC and both share the height from A. Mark each as half the whole. Second, the same argument applies to BE and to CF, so each median halves the triangle. Third, within triangle ABD, the segment from B through G to E and the segment from G to F cut it into three of the six small triangles. Applying the equal-base-and-common-height argument repeatedly shows all six small triangles have equal area, each one sixth of the whole. Label each with the fraction one sixth and add a note that this is why the centroid is the centre of mass of a uniform triangular plate. Also mark on one median that G divides it in the ratio 2 to 1 from the vertex, and note that this ratio is about lengths, not areas, since the areas are all equal.

items.stem: Prove that triangles on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area.
items.answer: Let ABC and ABD be two triangles on the same base AB, with the vertices C and D lying on a line that is parallel to AB. We must show that the two triangles have equal area. The area of a triangle is half the base times the perpendicular height, where the height is measured from the base to the opposite vertex. Both triangles have the same base AB, so it remains to show that they have the same height. Drop the perpendicular from C to the line AB, meeting it at H, and the perpendicular from D to AB, meeting it at K. Both CH and DK are perpendicular distances between the two parallel lines, the line AB and the line through C and D. The distance between two parallel lines is the same at every point, since that is what it means for lines to be parallel. Therefore CH equals DK, and the two triangles have the same height. Since both have base AB and equal heights, the area of ABC is half AB times CH and the area of ABD is half AB times DK, and these are equal. Hence triangles on the same base and between the same parallels have equal area. Two consequences are worth noting. First, the triangles need not be congruent, and in general they have quite different shapes and perimeters; only the areas match. Second, the same argument applied to parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels shows that they too have equal area, since each parallelogram is two such triangles.
